newsitem.title: UK: CRICKET-OLD AND NEW COMBINE TO SAVE ENGLAND.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-OLD AND NEW COMBINE TO SAVE ENGLAND.

text.p: Michael Atherton and Mark Butcher, the old and the new, combined in an opening partnership of 162 on Monday to deny Australia victory on the final day of the second Ashes test at Lord's.
The England duo, batting together for only the fourth time, laid the foundation for a second innings total of 266 for four declared.
Australia had declared their first innings at their overnight total of 213 for seven, a lead of 136.
Atherton, captaining his country for a record 42nd time, displayed his familiar qualities of grit and studious defence as Australia strove to equal the six-test Ashes series.
He reached 77 in 220 minutes with 10 boundaries, before treading on his off-stump after turning Michael Kasprowicz to fine-leg.

Surrey left-hander Butcher, in danger of losing his place after failing for the third time in England's first innings of 77 and dropping two catches on Saturday, survived through a combination of character, concentration and luck.

He was dropped on two by Mark Taylor at first slip off Paul Reiffel, looked fallible throughout on and outside the off-stump and could make little sense of Shane Warne's exotic wrist-spin from the Nursery end.

With the bounce lower and slower than on Saturday, Butcher perservered to reach 87 in 266 minutes with 14 boundaries before he was beaten and bowled by Warne with a delivery which turned sharply from the bowlers' rough.
"It was a good performance, it was a test of character for him," said Atherton. "The more he stayed the more confidence he got."
Warne gave Australia a glimpse of victory when he caught and bowled Nasser Hussain, scorer of a double-century in the first test, for a duck in the next over.
But Graham Thorpe (30 not out) and John Crawley (29 not out) extinguished their hopes on the only full day of play in the match with some pleasant strokes in the evening sunshine.

Australia, whose past 18 tests had not featured a single draw, took the field with the verve and determination which has seen them to series victories over West Indies and South Africa already this year.

But crucially Glenn McGrath, who wrecked England's first innings with eight for 38, could not summon the same demons from the relaid Lord's pitch while the left-handed Thorpe and Crawley successfully countered the threat of Warne.
With little more than two full days' cricket possible, both teams can take heart from the result.
Australia attacked throughout, McGrath and Matthew Elliott, who scored his maiden test century on Sunday, compared favourably with the heroes of the past and Warne looked to be returning to his best.
"Warney is improving," Taylor said. "We can only hope he can improve as much as he has in the last week."
England batted resolutely on Monday at a time, as Atherton conceded, when the only results possible were a draw or a win for Australia.
"We batted well and got out of a ptentially dodgy situation," Atherton said. "It was an unsatisfactory game for players and spectators, so much was lost through rain."
Taylor, who strove throughout to conjure an unlikely result, was upbeat about his team's prospects in the remaining four tests.
"There's no doubt that we can win three out of four matches," he said. "I am quite delighted at the way we came back in this match."
